title: Chapter 134 – The Rice Pot
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Su Qinghe]

Su Qinghe is seventy-five years old and she is not dying, and she will thank everyone to stop looking at her as if she were.

She says so to the pot. It is a large black iron rice pot with a dented lid, older than her second son, and she has stirred it every morning for fifty-two years. She says it to the wooden spoon, and to the string of dried peppers over the stove, and to the grandchildren who are hiding under the table pretending not to listen. She says it with her back straight and her hair pinned up and one hand braced, only a little, on the edge of the hearth.

"I fell," she says. "I did not die. People fall. There is no need for a pillow."

"Grandmother," says Little Bell, from under the table.

"Do not Grandmother me. I am making porridge."

There are fourteen children in the Garden kitchen this morning, ranging from Feng's youngest, who is four, to a gangling lad of thirteen who is a cousin's cousin and has been told off for eating the sugar. They watch her from behind the table legs like soldiers watching a general. She does not look at them. She stirs. The spoon scrapes the bottom of the pot with a sound she has known all her life.

The porridge smells of nothing.

She has noticed it before, in recent weeks. It is not that the food is bland. It is that it has begun to lose its edges, as if the world were being dusted over with ash. Salt is not quite salt. Ginger is not quite sharp. She has said nothing to anyone, because it is only an old woman's tongue, and there are nineteen things on the Garden's list before it.

She stirs again. The room swims.

It is only for a moment. The edges of the table go soft and gray, and she grips the hearth, and the spoon clatters out of her hand onto the stone. She hears the children gasp. She hears a chair scrape. She hears her own breath, thin and high, like wind through a keyhole.

"Grandmother!"

"I am well," says Qinghe, to the room. And then, because there is nobody there but the pot, and she is very tired: "I am so tired."

* * *

The Garden is not the Garden she married into, and she knows it as she makes her morning round with a basket on her arm.

Five hundred and sixty-two people. She counts them as Wenyuan counts them, in the dark, by habit. The Seat has its own gate now, a broad arch of gray stone with a carved lintel, and the Garden Hall is no longer the crooked old barn she remembers; it has a tiled roof and two wings and a bell tower. There is a school for the children, run by a nervous young man from the Sutra Hall who is terrified of Yue. There is a clinic, with a sign over the door in a hand she knows. There are forty new houses along the lower terrace, whitewashed, with smoke curling from their chimneys, and a smithy, and a mill. Hu's grandson runs the mill. He has his grandfather's ears.

Wenqing's boy keeps the grain-books. Wenshi's girl runs the dyers' row. Feng's eldest is a Foundation Establishment cultivator at twenty-six, with a stubborn jaw and a grave, serious manner that reminds her uncomfortably of someone she once carried through a famine winter. He bows to her in the lane. She tells him to eat properly.

At the lower gate she meets Kuang, in his Inner Sect sash, leaning on a staff. He is forty-four. He has put on weight. He has a gray streak in his beard and a squint, and he regards her with the expression of a man deciding whether to salute.

"Mother Lin," he says.

"I am not your mother."

"I know. It is the nearest word." He ducks his head. "I heard you fell."

"I descended."

"Bai said that too." His mouth twitches. "He is worried about you."

"He is ninety-three and he should be worried about himself." She shifts the basket. "How is the Hall?"

"Quiet." He looks out over the terraces. "Too quiet, since the Offering. The Registry is a rumor. The Head sleeps. Wuping is a decent man with a very poor poker face." He hesitates. "I keep thinking someone will come out of the dark. I have been thinking it for ten years."

"Has anyone?"

"No." He rubs his beard. "That is what frightens me."

She pats his arm. It is a thick arm, hard as a root. "Eat properly," she says.

"Yes, Mother Lin."

"Stop that."

"Yes, Mother Lin."

She walks on. Behind her, in the lane, she hears him laugh: a big, loud, sudden laugh that rings off the stones like a dropped pan, and she thinks, for no reason she can explain, that it is a sound her son used to know.

* * *

Bai is carried into the Garden Hall on a litter, on the first day of the ninth month, protesting every step.

"I can walk."

"You cannot," says Feng, who is fifty-five and broad and graying and carries the front of the litter without noticeable effort. "You fell off the stool in the Pill Hall yesterday."

"I did not fall. I descended."

"Onto the floor."

"At a controlled speed." Bai folds his arms. He is ninety-three, and he has shrunk to a bundle of sticks in a gray robe, with a face like a dried apple and a pair of thick lenses mended with wire. His hands lie in his lap like two small trembling birds. But the eyes behind the glass, as they were sixty years ago, are sharp as flint. "Put me down. Gently. I am a precious relic."

They set him down at the long table. He looks around at the circle of faces: Wenyuan, bent and silver-haired, in his lined gloves; Feng; Hu, who has gone entirely gray; Yue, thirty-five, with a ledger and a little girl on her knee; a dozen of the council. Last of all, at the foot, Qinghe, small and upright, with her hands folded.

"Well," says Bai. "Here we are."

"You wished to speak," says Wenyuan.

"I wished to announce." The old man raises one trembling finger. "In sixty years I have made a great many pills. Some for killing, some for curing, one for making a mule sing. I have never made one for love. I am about to make one now, and I wish it understood that I will not be dissuaded."

Nobody says a word.

"The Foundation pill is ready," says Bai. "The base is in my jar. I have it at the fourth stage, and if I do not complete it this winter I shall not finish it at all. The companion herb is in the east bed, and Qinghe herself grew it. Nine Turn, from seed, twelve years. I have been waiting for it to flower." He lowers his finger. "It flowered last week."

Qinghe stares at him.

"You did not tell me."

"I did not wish you to worry." Bai coughs, a dry thin rattle. "It is a sad old woman who watches a flower to see whether she will live."

"I was not watching."

"You were watering it at dawn and dusk with a measuring cup." The old man's mouth twitches. "I have eyes, girl. I am old, not dead."

There is a long, appalled silence. And then, to her own astonishment, Qinghe begins to laugh. She laughs until the tears come, a thin high rusty cackle that sets the children laughing under the table and Wenyuan wiping his eyes with his glove.

"Very well," she says, when she can speak. "I am watched."

"You are loved," says Bai. "It is the same thing, only more tiresome."

* * *

Her son comes home on the nineteenth of the ninth month, at dusk, with the rain.

She is on the porch. She has been on the porch since noon, in a blanket, with a bowl of beans in her lap, and she has told every child who passed that she is shelling beans. She has shelled none. She sits with the bowl on her knees and watches the road, and the road is empty, and the rain is coming down in long gray sheets.

Then a figure appears at the bottom of the lane.

It is a tall man in a patched traveler's cloak, with a pack on his back, walking slowly. A gray man. His hair is the color of ash, cropped short. His face is lined and lean and weathered, with deep creases at the eyes and mouth, and he walks with a slight stoop. A small gray animal rides on his shoulder with a bell at her neck. And behind him, forty paces back, a line of ragged men in dull gray: a dozen, silent, soaked.

She knows him by his walk.

Su Qinghe has lived seventy-five years and she has never run. But she is off the porch and down the steps and out into the mud before she knows she has moved, her blanket falling away behind her, her slippers sinking. She is halfway down the lane when she realizes that he has seen her. He has stopped walking. He stands in the road with the rain streaming off his face, and the little animal on his shoulder is quite still, and something in his posture, the lifted head, the open hands, makes her think of a child who has come home too late.

"You are thin," she says.

It is the first thing that comes to her tongue. It comes out hoarse.

"I know."

"And gray."

"Yes."

"And you are walking like an old man, Lin Jian. I was told you were Purple Mansion. I was told you would live three hundred years. Why do you walk like an old man?"

He does not answer. He lets his pack slide off his shoulder into the mud. And then she is in his arms, small as a bird, with her face against his wet chest and her hands knotted in his cloak, and she is sobbing like a girl.

"Twelve years," she says. "Twelve years. You said a few."

"I said I did not know."

"I counted the days." She pushes him back, takes his face in both hands, studies it with fierce, streaming eyes. "You have a new line. Here. And here. Who gave you that?" She frowns. "You do not remember. You have forgotten something. I can see it. You have the look of a man who has put his hand in his pocket and found it empty."

"A few things."

"What things?"

He smiles. It is the same smile, the one he wore at six when he had broken a bowl. "I have your spoon," he says. "I did not lose that."

* * *

They put him to work at once.

"I have been fed seventeen years of rumor," says Bai, in the dim crowded warmth of the Pill Hall, with a candle at his elbow and a jar the size of a man's head open before him. "I do not care where you have been or what you have eaten. I care that you have a vault of two hundred units and a bench that can print a pill. Show me."

Jian has gone to the Dock. He has been gone since dawn. Now he is back, and he stands in the door with a shadow in his face that Qinghe cannot name, and says, quite plainly: "One hundred and four."

"Four more than I need."

"It is what the Reservoir took. I did not control it." He looks at his mother. She is propped in a chair by the stove, in a shawl. "Mother. It is more than half the vault. Ninety-six remain. The Vein will refill the rest in two winters, if the frost is kind."

"Then it is a very good thing," says Qinghe tartly, "that you are not going anywhere."

He opens his mouth. Closes it.

"I have said it," she adds, "and I will not say it twice. You are staying until I am out of the cocoon. I do not care what is on the other side of the world. I do not care if the sky is falling in. You will sit at that table, and you will eat what I give you, and you will sleep in your own bed until I tell you to leave."

"Four months."

"Four months." She lifts her chin. "I have waited ten years. You can wait four."

Bai makes a small dry sound that may be a laugh. Across the room Wenyuan, in his gloves, in the corner, has bowed his head, and his shoulders are shaking.

* * *

The pill is the size of a plum stone and the color of old amber, and it sits in her palm like a drop of honey.

It is not what she expected. She had braced for something monstrous, a black lump, a bitter horse-pill. Instead it is warm and faintly sweet-smelling, like a baker's window in winter. Bai has wrapped the Nine Turn blossom around it in a twist of leaf. The flower is small and white, with nine delicate spiral petals, and she grew it. She had put the seed in the earth with her own hands, twelve years ago, on a morning when the frost was on the ground, and told it in a whisper that it had better be worth the trouble.

"It is very pretty," she says.

"It is bitter," says Bai. "Swallow it quickly."

"And then?"

"And then you sleep. For four months, more or less. You will be in the cocoon room, on a mat, with a lamp. You will not wake. Your breath will go thin and slow. You will dream." The old man's face softens. "You will not be alone. I will sit with you."

"You are ninety-three."

"I am a stubborn ninety-three." He pats her hand with his small trembling fingers. "Do not argue, child. It is the last thing I shall ever make. I should like to see it work."

She looks at the pill. She looks at the circle of faces round the room, dim in the candlelight: her husband, her sons, her daughter, the children peering round the door. She looks at the tall gray man at the back, with a hand on his sister's shoulder, whom she once carried under her heart for ten months and rocked all through one long winter when he would not stop screaming.

"If I do not wake," she says.

"You will wake."

"If I do not." She turns to Wenyuan. "You will eat properly. You will let Feng's wife cut your hair. And you will not, under any circumstances, let Hu teach the grandchildren any of his songs."

"Qinghe—"

"Promise."

"I promise," says Wenyuan, and his voice cracks.

She nods once. Then she puts the pill on her tongue, and swallows, and it is bitter beyond bitter, a taste like burnt iron and cold ashes and the bottom of a well. She makes a face. Somebody laughs. She hears Bai say, good, good, and feels the mat beneath her, and the dark come up like water.

* * *

She dreams of the Orchard.

It is spring. The apple trees are in flower, a white drift across the hill, and she is nineteen, in a blue skirt, carrying a basket of eggs to the market. The air smells of grass and honey. A boy is leaning on the wall by the road, a broad-shouldered boy with a farmer's hands and an anxious face, and he straightens when he sees her. He has been waiting. He does not say so.

"You are late," he says.

"I am not."

"I have been here an hour."

"Then you are early." She stops, shifts the basket. "What do you want, Wenyuan?"

"To carry that."

"It is eggs."

"I will be very careful." He holds out his arms. His ears are red. "I am a careful man."

She hands him the basket. He takes it as though it were made of glass. They walk down the road together between the white trees, and she thinks, with perfect clarity, that she is going to marry this boy, and that it will not be easy, and that she will not mind.

The Orchard fades. She is in the kitchen, and it is night, and there is a baby on her knee. It is her second, a quiet one, with a tuft of dark hair. He is not crying. He is looking at the lamp. She has had him two days, and he has not yet made a sound, and she is frightened, and Wenyuan is behind her with his big hand on her shoulder, saying, Well, little stone, you'll sink us all.

The baby laughs.

She wakes with the sound in her ears. She does not know how long she has slept. The lamp has burned down. It is dark, and cold, and the mat beneath her is wet with sweat, and somewhere beside her, very close, a thin old voice is humming. A tuneless, tender little hum, the sort an old man makes when he thinks nobody is awake.

"Bai," she whispers.

"Sleep, girl," says the voice. "It is only the middle."

* * *

In the middle of the third month she half-wakes and hears them talking.

It is deep night. The lamp is low. She cannot open her eyes, cannot move her hands, cannot do more than lie in the heavy warm dark with her ear turned toward the voices. Two men, close, on either side of the mat, speaking softly so as not to wake her. She knows them both by the breathing.

"You are tired," says Wenyuan.

"I am not."

"You have not slept in two nights. You have sat in that chair like a post." There is the clink of a cup. "Drink this."

"Father—"

"Drink."

A pause. A swallow. "It is terrible."

"It is barley. Your mother makes it. She would be insulted." The old man's voice is gentle, even a little amused. "Jian. May I say a thing?"

"Of course."

"I have been watching you for a week. You have a look I know. I had it myself, the winter after the Orchard fell. A man who has put down something very large and cannot remember where." A silence. "You do not have to tell me what it is. I only wish you to know that you may. And that I will not think less."

For a long time there is no answer. She hears the lamp sputter. She hears her son's breath, uneven.

"Father," he says at last. "When I was born. Did I cry?"

"No."

"Mother says I looked at the lamp."

"You did." Wenyuan's voice shakes. "I thought there was something wrong with you. The midwife said to wait. We waited an hour. And then you turned your head and looked at me, directly, as though you had a question. And I said—" He stops.

"Well, little stone."

"You remember."

"No. Mother told me." A very long pause. "I wished to hear it again."

"Well, little stone," says Wenyuan softly, "you'll sink us all."

"And I laughed."

"You laughed. Two days old. I thought, this one is going to be trouble." She hears the old man's breath hitch, and then a dry sound like paper rustling. "I was right. And I have never been so glad of anything."

Another silence. When her son speaks, his voice is so quiet that she has to strain.

"Thank you for saying it."

"I will say it every night, if you wish."

"I do not deserve you."

"No," says Wenyuan, cheerfully. "But I am here anyway." The chair creaks. A warm hand, a cold glove, settles on her forehead and smooths back her hair. "Sleep, Jian. I will watch her. It is my turn."

She lies in the dark and listens to her son weep without a sound, and her husband pat his shoulder with a gloved hand, and she thinks, drifting down again into sleep, that of all the pills in the world, of all the grand cold clever things Bai ever made, this is the only one that really works.

* * *

On the last night of the fourth month, Bai dies.

She does not see it. She is deep in the cocoon, in the roots of the dark, and what she knows of it she learns afterward, from Yue, in a quiet voice. He had sat by her mat every night for a hundred and nineteen nights, on a stool, with a blanket over his knees, and a candle, and a bowl of barley water. He had watched her breath. He had changed the cloths. He had hummed. On the hundred and nineteenth night, at the third watch, he had stopped humming.

When the dawn came, Hu found him, upright on the stool, with his chin on his chest and his spectacles slipped down his nose. He had a small, tight, stubborn smile. In his lap, folded in a clean cloth, lay a candied plum.

Qinghe wakes at noon, in the heat, with the sun on her face.

She lies for a long time with her eyes closed, listening. There is no hum. The room is quiet. She feels, in her belly, a warm, steady, unfamiliar light, as though a lamp had been lit there and left to burn. She breathes in and the breath goes down deep, deeper than it has ever gone, into corners she did not know she had. Her hands are strong. Her back does not ache. There is no dizziness.

She opens her eyes.

Jian is sitting on the stool.

He is gray and unshaven, with dark circles under his eyes, and his hands are folded between his knees. He has been there a long time. She can see it. He looks up and sees her awake, and something goes across his face, relief, grief, a kind of helpless joy, and he cannot speak.

"Foundation," says Qinghe. Her voice is a thread.

"Yes. Early."

"I feel..." She cannot find the word. "I feel I could lift the roof."

"Please do not."

She almost smiles. Then she sees the candied plum. It sits on the stool-seat between his hands, in its square of cloth, small and sticky and amber, and she knows at once where it came from.

"Bai," she says.

He doesn't answer. He picks up the plum and holds it out.

She takes it. The sugar is cold. She puts it in her mouth, and she waits for the sweetness, the sharp bright shock of it, the smell of old kitchens and warm boxes. She waits. It does not come.

It is ash.

It is a small, soft, damp lump of ash, with no more taste than a pebble. She chews. She swallows. She lies back on the mat with the empty cloth in her hand, and tears run from the corners of her eyes down into her ears, and she cannot stop them.

"It was the last thing he made," she says.

"I know."

"I cannot taste it."

"I know, Mother."

"I will never taste it again, will I? Not Bai's plums. Not your father's soup. Not anything." She is crying openly now, hoarse and helpless. "Is that the price?"

"I think so."

"I thought it would be something worse." She wipes her face with the heel of her hand. "I thought it would be one of you." She laughs wetly. "It is only my tongue."

"It is not only your tongue." His voice is very low. "It is every dinner. Every birthday. Every winter pot of rice you will cook for the next hundred years and never taste."

She looks at him. She looks at the gray head, and the lines, and the hands, and the child behind them who looked at the lamp and did not cry.

"Jian," she says. "Listen to me. I am seventy-five years old. I have a hundred and twenty more. I will see Little Bell married. I will see her children. I will cook for them all, and I will burn some of it, and nobody will have the heart to tell me." She takes his hand. "I will pay that price every day, gladly, for the rest of my life. And I will not have you carry it."

He bows his head. His shoulders shake.

She holds his hand and does not let go. Outside, in the Garden, someone has begun to ring a bell. A plain iron bell, ringing slow, for the old man in the Pill Hall who died on a stool with his spectacles slipping.

It is the ordinary bell. It is the wrong bell for a death. And it is the most beautiful sound she has ever heard.
